statement: The overall Gravatar design reuses the photo upload service designed in the previous lecture unchanged (pre-signed URL and the rest); when the user publishes a photo, an entry is made in the photos table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we take the photo upload service that we designed yesterday, plug and play as it over here. No changes at all.

statement: In the Gravatar schema, a published photo row holds the user ID and is_active = true, and the users table stores the email and the hash of the email.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: User ID, is active as true. Schema, users, you store email and the hash.

statement: Gravatar stores a derived value (the email hash), contrary to the previous lecture's advice not to store derivable data, because it makes the index lookup faster.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: here we are storing the derived value because it makes index look up faster

statement: Gravatar photos should not be served from the backend servers but via a CDN: at Facebook or Instagram scale (millions of hits), all that traffic hitting the backend and then S3 would create chaos and the AWS bill would shoot up; a CDN also gives a better user experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now we do not want to serve photos from our backend servers. We want to serve via CDN.

statement: The Gravatar backend exposes an API endpoint api.gravatar.com/photo/<hash>: for the given hash it finds the active photo, reads the file from S3 and returns it in the response.
detail: The teacher calls this the standard procedure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we expose an API endpoint called api.gravatar.com slash photo slash hash.

statement: The S3 path of a photo is derived on the fly from the user ID and the photo ID rather than stored.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we derive the S3 path on the fly because we know the user ID and we know the photos ID.

statement: To have the CDN serve the photos, a CDN property gravatar.com is configured whose origin is api.gravatar.com/photos (the API endpoint that reads the photo from S3 and returns it).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what we do is we configure gravatar.com and origin to that is api.gravatar.com slash photos.

statement: Unlike the previous lecture's CDN setup with a subdomain property (edge.arpitbhayani.me), for Gravatar the root domain gravatar.com itself is the CDN property.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: My root domain itself is my property on CDN.

statement: Request flow: a request for gravatar.com/<hash> goes to the CDN; on a hit the CDN serves it; on a miss it goes to the origin api.gravatar.com, which reads the photo from S3 and returns it; the CDN caches it and serves the user, and subsequent requests are served from the CDN.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If CDN has the data, it would serve it. If it does not have the data, it would go to origin.

statement: Basic Gravatar upload flow: upload the photo to S3 using a pre-signed URL, then call the API server to register the photo in the database (MySQL, or any database you prefer).
detail: The teacher calls it a very basic flow, nothing super complicated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You upload a photo using pre-signed URL on S3.

statement: When a photo is published or updated, the API server updates the database and pushes an event to Kafka.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We update it in the DB and push an event to Kafka.

statement: The Kafka event exists to invalidate the CDN cache: once user 2 has loaded user 1's photo through the CDN, it is served from the CDN to everyone, so when user 1 updates the photo the cached copy must be invalidated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Right, now why Kafka? Because we want to invalidate the cache

statement: Because photos do not change often, the CDN TTL for Gravatar photos might be one or two days.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because photos don't change that often, you might have a TTL of let's say one day or two day or something like that.

statement: Even with a long TTL, when a user changes the photo it should be invalidated in the CDN right away so the new photo renders, for a good user experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: as to give a good user experience, you want to invalidate that photo right there and then, so that the new photo is rendered.

statement: The photo-updated event in Kafka goes to a bunch of consumers (workers) whose only job is to invalidate the CDN: they call the CDN's API to invalidate the path (e.g. /h1); the next request misses, goes to the API server, which reads the S3 path from the DB, reads the file from S3 and sends it to the CDN, which caches and serves it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it goes to a bunch of consumers whose job is to invalidate the CDN. That's it.

statement: CDNs expose APIs to invalidate a particular path.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN gives you those API so invalidate a particular path.

statement: Gravatar is a simple system; what makes it interesting are the details: how the CDN is leveraged, how database transactions are used, how the schema evolved, asking critical questions, and keeping security and correctness of the data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a very simple system, but these details make it very interesting.

statement: In the mark-active transaction, if a wrong photo ID is passed, the user ID condition in the update prevents touching another user's photo: no rows are updated.
detail: A student asked what happens inside the transaction if a wrong photo ID is passed to the query that sets a photo active.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that's why we have this user ID to prevent that, right? So no rows update, it would happen.

statement: If an update is expected to change something but changes nothing, that is an alarm; in most cases it means a bug, e.g. in the front end.
detail: Raised by a student's general question: should a transaction have a fallback if one query gets a wrong parameter and matches nothing?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So let's say a general behavior is something gets updated, but you saw that nothing got updated. That is an alarm for you.

statement: With a wrong photo ID, the transaction's first update sets all the user's photos inactive and the second activates nothing, so the user has no active photo and gets a 404.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's a, that's a 404. That's a 404 for user.

statement: If the invariant is that a user has exactly one active photo, the transaction must check it: first select the photo row with that photo ID and user ID, and only if it exists run the two updates; otherwise do nothing.
detail: The teacher also mentions checking that at least one photo is active.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If that row exists, then only you do these two. Otherwise you don't.
flags: unclear: "It with Matt meets that day"

statement: Always validate that the changes you are about to make cannot leave the data in an inconsistent state: check first, then write.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it is always better to just validate that whatever changes that you are doing will not let your data go in inconsistent state.

statement: A student suggested splitting the handling in two: if zero rows come back, application logic reports that the ID was not found, while a failed transaction rolls back by itself.
detail: No explicit verdict from the teacher.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if the row, zero rows return, then application logic take care of saying that ID was not one at all

statement: CDN mapping recap: a request to gravatar.com goes to the CDN (as edge.arpitbhayani.me did in the previous lecture); the CDN's origin is api.gravatar.com, so on a miss the CDN calls the API server.
detail: A student had read the mapping in reverse order.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it goes to CDN and CDN's origin is configured to API to gravatar.com.
flags: check: "API.com." may be a student's answer - teacher replies "No, no."

statement: A common question is why the CDN does not point to S3 directly; one reason given is that S3 is not public.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One common question that ask is why CDN not pointing to S3 directly? Because S3 is not public.

statement: S3 does not know which photo is active; only the database is the source of truth for that, so the CDN falls back to api.gravatar.com, which reads the database, finds the active photo, fetches it from S3 and sends it to the CDN.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: S3 doesn't know which photo is active. Right? Only database is a source of truth for it to know which photo is active.

statement: Hashing at query time is ruled out because with a WHERE clause like hash(email) = X the database must go through every row, compute the hash of each email and compare it: a full table scan.
detail: Answer to a student who did not understand why runtime hashing should not be done.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: compute the hash of the email ID, see if it matches with the thing that you passed. That is a full table scan.

statement: In the active-photo query, the join on user ID is only a join criterion (it is the foreign key), not a filter; the input from the URL is the hash, so the user ID is not needed up front.
detail: A student asked why the query cannot filter on user ID directly instead of the hash.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We don't need user ID. We just a join criteria because it's a foreign key.

statement: The query narrows step by step: the filter on the user hash yields one candidate row from users; it is joined on that user ID to photos, matching e.g. the 10 photos uploaded; then the is-active filter leaves the active photo.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: from which you'll get just one row as candidate match from the users table

statement: The database query optimizer decides which part to evaluate first; here it finds the unique key on the user hash and evaluates that first, then applies the join criterion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your database query optimizer takes care of which one to evaluate first.

statement: Predicate pushdown is how SQL engines optimise queries: filters are pushed to the bottom (leaf nodes) of the evaluation tree, so they are applied first, then the join, then the rest going up.
detail: The teacher suggests Googling predicate pushdown.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is called as predicate pushdown.

statement: A query evaluation tree is evaluated from the bottom to the top.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because a tree evaluates from the bottom to the top.

statement: The CDN cache is invalidated on an image update by calling the CDN's API: Cloudflare, Akamai and every CDN expose invalidation APIs.
detail: A student asked how the cache is invalidated when the image is updated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Cloudflare, Akamai, every CDN has APIs exposed to invalidate the cache.

statement: Gravatar does not rely on the TTL but invalidates the cache up front, because user experience matters: after a photo change the user wants to see the new photo everywhere immediately.
detail: A student restated it as 'invalidating directly by calling the CDN'; the teacher answered 'Correct. Synchronous. Yes.', while the design shown earlier uses Kafka consumers to make the call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because user experience really matters over here that when the photo is changed, I want to immediately see the uploaded photo everywhere.
flags: check: teacher says "Synchronous" although the design uses Kafka consumers

statement: Agenda: adding the active photo ID optimization is already covered; next is on-demand image optimization, then questions, then a break.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What we'll do is we'll talk a bit about on-demand image optimization and then we take questions and then we go on a break.

statement: Once you know how a CDN and Gravatar work, on-demand image optimization becomes a piece of cake.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now that you know how CDN works, you know how Gravatar works, on-demand image optimization becomes a piece of cake.

statement: The problem: the same image is needed at many sizes, e.g. a Facebook profile photo as a tiny 16x16 or 32x32 dot on one page, 256x256 on another, 512x512 on another; the user uploads at any resolution and the size requested should be served.
detail: Assumes the CDN does not offer this feature.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But on other page, it is like 256 by 256. On some other page, it would be 512 by 512, something like that.

statement: On-demand image optimization is not the approach of uploading the image, posting a message and having a bunch of servers pre-create multiple variants; images are transformed when requested.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'll upload the image, I'll post it as a message and have a bunch of servers optimizing it and creating multiple variants of it.

statement: Like a CDN, the service accepts query parameters such as w=32, meaning transform the image to 32 pixels wide.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just like how CDN accepts query parameters, we would also accept query parameters like w equal to 32.

statement: In the Gravatar flow the CDN reads the URL and returns the file if it has it; otherwise the request (with its query parameters) goes to the origin, which reads the image from S3, applies the transformation passed in the query parameters and sends it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Origin would go to S3, read the image.

statement: ImageMagick is the world's most popular image processing library.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: like ImageMagick. This is the world's most popular image processing library out there.

statement: The Python Image Library (PIL) has two bindings: a native Python binding and ImageMagick.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Python image library PIL has two bindings. One is native Python binding. Second is ImageMagick.

statement: ImageMagick is written purely in C++, and almost every language has C++ bindings, so ImageMagick can be invoked natively from your preferred language.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ImageMagick is purely written in C++.

statement: Resizing with ImageMagick: call its native resize function (image.resize with the new size), get in-memory bytes back and send them to the user; this is the only change to the flow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It has a native resize function. Image.resize and you pass the new size.

statement: The origin supports whatever transformations you choose (grayscale, resizing, etc.) from the query parameters: get the image (from S3 if not present), apply the transformations with ImageMagick and return it as the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: pass the transformation, whatever you would want to support, grayscale, resizing and whatnot.

statement: This is exactly what CDNs do with transformation query parameters (covered in the previous lecture); the design re-implements it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is exactly what CDN also does.

statement: Image processing, encryption and video processing are very CPU-intensive workloads; you need a large amount of CPU, so you pay your cloud provider for bulky machines with many CPUs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: image processing, encryption, video processing, these are all very heavy CPU based, it's very CPU intensive workloads

statement: On-demand (not asynchronous) processing needs bulky machines because many CPUs let you parallelise and finish quickly; every on-demand image optimization or on-demand processing system is built this way, nothing fancy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you need to have bulky machines to do that because large number of CPUs, you can parallelize a lot of stuff

statement: On-demand image optimization cannot be made async because it is a synchronous request: when the URL is loaded, the response (e.g. a 240-pixel image) must be produced right then.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it cannot be made async because this is a synchronous request.

statement: Cloudflare or Cloudinary (the teacher is unsure which) published one of the shortest blogs he has read on this: they use the ImageMagick library on massive servers (32 or 64 cores or so) and scale the fleet with incoming requests. He read it six or seven years back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It literally said we use ImageMagick library, this, and run on massive servers, 30, 32 cores or 64 cores or something like that, right?

statement: Handling scale for synchronous image processing today is a no-brainer: you need large servers; there is nothing magic about on-demand image optimization.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is nothing magic when it comes to on-demand image optimization.

statement: Asynchronous processing will be discussed in about six weeks, with video streaming.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll talk in six weeks when we discuss video streaming a bit of it

statement: Build it: take two days and implement, step by step as one local prototype, exactly the sequence covered from 9 AM to 10:30 AM; you will then have no questions about CDNs, image processing or building these synchronous pieces.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: take two days of your time and implement those exact same things, the exact same way, step by step, just one local prototype

statement: There is not much more to image optimization: it is about bulky servers autoscaled on the incoming requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's all about having bulky servers to do that and autoscaling them depending on the requests that are coming in.

statement: Cloud providers give these facilities out of the box; very few engineers work on a team that manages its own such infrastructure, so it is typically abstracted away and we focus on things that matter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Cloud providers give you those facilities anywhere out of the box.
flags: check: "a team that manages its own app" - object of "manages" unclear

statement: With the active-photo-ID optimisation, marking a photo active becomes a single query on the users table: update users set active_photo_id = <photo> where hash = <hash>.
detail: A student checked that after the optimisation the active photo is fetched with a select on users by hash; the teacher answered by writing the update query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Update users set active photo ID equal to something where hash is equal to something.
flags: check: student asked about the select query, teacher wrote the update query

statement: Instead of a Boolean is_active, an integer-based enum is also fine and gives the flexibility to add a third state later, as long as it is stored as a tiny int.
detail: A student proposed storing state as an enum type rather than a Boolean for future flexibility; the teacher agreed.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So you can go for enum and integer based enum that does it for you.

statement: A Boolean takes 8 bits (1 byte) to store; the teacher first said 8 bytes and corrected himself to 8 bits.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And 8 bytes is 1 byte, 8 bits, 8 bits, I wanted to say 8 bits.

statement: Use a tiny int rather than a big integer for such state columns, and do not store the state as a string in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But just go with a tiny int rather than a big one. Don't store string as is in the database.

statement: Before the mark-active update, check that the photo ID belongs to this user (get, then update); the teacher says you 100% should, and skipped it only to avoid rewriting the queries.
detail: A student proposed improving the update with a join on the other table to verify the ID.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Yeah, 100% you should do that.

statement: Security has to hold at every step: if you take care of it in one place and lapse in another, it does not work; first get and check, then update.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if we take care of security over here and we lapse over here, that would not work, right?

statement: The Slack design used a separate membership table between users and channels while Gravatar's photos table just references the user; both are one-to-many, but the membership table stored extra per-user details (e.g. last read checkpoint, channel starred by the user), and Gravatar has no such complexity.
detail: A student suggested the reason was one-to-one vs one-to-many; the teacher said 'Brilliant. You gave the answer' but noted Gravatar is also one-to-many.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But there we were storing other details as well on that.
flags: check: teacher calls the student's answer brilliant and then says it is also one-to-many

statement: After the break: tagging people in photos, not to design the (easy) system but to show how a simple system affects many other systems; then the newly unread message indicator.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What I want to highlight through this system is how this simple system affects so many other systems, right?

statement: Senior engineers are responsible not just for building one system but for seeing how it interacts with and could affect other systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are not just responsible for building this one system today, but rather seeing how it affects, how it interacts with other system

statement: Typical startup scenario: a CXO says 'let's allow people to tag people in photos' and that one line is the entire product briefing you get to implement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's allow people to tag people in photos. That's all, that's your product briefing.

statement: A senior engineer must think of what senior management has not thought of (more common than you think); they trust your instinct, and the hard part is not the high level but how the feature fits into the bigger puzzle.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now a senior engineer, you need to think of senior management has not thought of. Unfortunately, that's true. More common than you think.

statement: The exercise: think only about requirements, not the solution, wearing the product manager's hat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We will not talk about solution. Not talk about solution at all.

statement: A senior engineer always wears three hats at once: product manager, architect and engineer; together they create synergy.
detail: The teacher says he will repeat this next week and the week after.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Senior engineer always wears three hats. First is a hat of a product manager.

statement: Product manager hat: requirements, things others have not thought about, bringing clarity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Requirements, things that others have not thought about, bringing in that clarity.

statement: Architect hat: architect the system with its future extensibility in mind.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Second is a hat of an architect where you're supposed to architect a system considering extensibility of it in the future.

statement: Engineer hat: go into the low-level nitty-gritty details and ensure the system is optimal across all layers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the hat of an engineer, which goes into those low level nitty gritty details of it and ensures that it is optimal

statement: Given the one-line brief, brainstorm what questions you would ask yourself or your team (not the manager), one question per person.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What questions would you ask not to manager but to yourself, to your team or how would you brainstorm about it?
flags: asr: [?wear the first hat | asr: "bear the first hand"]

statement: A student's first requirements question was what the schema for storing tags should be.
detail: Correction: nothing around engineering at this stage; given only the one-line brief, think on the product side.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Nothing around engineering. Nothing around engineering. Don't think on engineering at all.

statement: A student proposed that only the photo's owner can tag, so nobody tags the wrong people or objects.
detail: Correction: owner-only tagging is an obvious check; do not go into correctness of tags. More important is authorization: who is allowed to tag me in their photos, a control the tagged user should have.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So what you should more focus on is authorization part, where who can tag me in their photo.
flags: check: "yes, that's ... right" may be the student's interjection

statement: Tagging needs a separate authorization layer that tracks who is allowed to tag a user in their photos, as on Instagram or Twitter where you may not be allowed to tag some people.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Which means that now you have to have a separate authorization layer, which keeps track of things that, hey, am I allowed to tag?

statement: A student raised the maximum number of people that can be tagged in a photo (also asking photo vs album/collection level; the teacher kept it at photo level).
detail: The student also listed removing one's own tag; the teacher took one point at a time.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I would prefer how many people can be tagged in a photo.

statement: A student said a limit of five would require managing concurrent tag updates by several people.
detail: Correction: only the owner tags people in their own photo; someone else cannot tag in your photo, so concurrency is not a challenge here.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So concurrency is not a challenge here.
flags: check: speaker - "Student 3" replies after Student 5 proposal

statement: The max tag limit determines the storage schema: with a limit of five, the tagged people can be kept directly in an array.
detail: The teacher contrasts extremes, 5 vs 10,000.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it is just five people, you can go and keep them in an array directly.

statement: With a limit of 10,000, tagged people need separate entries: a single document would grow too big (as discussed in the previous lecture), and you would need paginated endpoints since no one needs 10,000 in one shot.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if it is 10,000, you would need to have separate entries for them
flags: asr: [?would have to | asr: "won't have to"]

statement: Every requirement question should lead to a change in, or positively influence, the design.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single question that we ask leads to a change, affects or rather should positively influence our design.

statement: A student proposed notifying tagged people; the teacher agreed: otherwise someone could tag you in a very bad photo without you knowing.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Otherwise, otherwise just imagine someone tagging you in a very shitty photo and you don't even know about it.
flags: check: "If I say yes, then" may be the teacher

statement: If tagged people are notified, interface with the notification team before rollout: they will see a huge traffic spike as people start tagging, so they must get ready to scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would see a huge spike on your traffic as soon as people start to use this feature

statement: If the notification system is not scaled up before the tag notifications are pushed, it gets overburdened and other critical notifications might be affected.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Other critical notifications might get affected.

statement: Tag notifications also need product-level throttling, distinct from system throttling: users hate apps that over-notify, and a daily notification is a big turn-off that can lead to uninstalls.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is basically product level throttling.

statement: Good apps send only about three to five notifications a week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: People, good apps only send three notifications a week or five notifications.

statement: Notifying a user for every single post they are tagged in is a bad user experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Getting notifications for every single post you are tagged in is a bad user experience.

statement: Ask the notification team whether they throttle (add it if not), do not bombard users with a notification per tagged photo: club them and give a rich notification experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You need to ensure that you are not bombarding other users with notifications for every photo that they are tagged in. Club them.

statement: A student's example: when a very famous celebrity posts a photo and many people tag them, they would get lots of notifications; the teacher agreed.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: very famous celebrity posted one photo and other people are tag, tagging

statement: Senior management may well have not thought it through; given a one-line statement, it is your responsibility to dissect it, go into the details and point them out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now it's your responsibility to dissect it and go into those details and point them.

statement: A student proposed a profile setting for whether anyone can tag me; the teacher said this is covered by the first point (who can tag).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: in the like profile settings, whether anyone can tag me or not.
flags: check: "did that first point, first" may be the teacher interjecting
asr: [?who can tag | asr: "who can that"]

statement: A student proposed self-removal of tags; the teacher agreed: if people tag you in, say, an obscene photo, you should be able to remove yourself.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Let's say in some obscene photo people tagged you. You should have an option to remove yourself from that.

statement: Self-removal makes authorization more granular: the photo belongs to user one, yet a tagged user may remove themselves from it, which requires a very robust authorization layer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now this requires you to build a very robust authorization layer.

statement: A student proposed tag suggestions ("this photo looks like this person from your friends list", as Facebook does), which needs face recognition and recommendation ML systems; on a photo upload event their inputs are fetched and shown to the user.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: whether we would have suggestions, okay, this photo looks like this person from your friends list, something that Facebook does, I think.

statement: Showing tag suggestions needs front-end changes and a fast suggestion service: if the ML service is slow, users sometimes see suggestions and sometimes not, a poor experience; the ML team must maintain a certain SLA.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It maintains a certain SLA.

statement: Suggestions create a synchronous dependency on the ML team's API (suggestions must appear as soon as the user starts tagging), so that API needs a very strict SLA it adheres to.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now you have a synchronous dependency on the team

statement: With a synchronous dependency you need a fallback plan for when the API does not respond in time, e.g. block tagging or allow manual tagging.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And now you also need to create a fallback plan. What if that API does not respond in time?

statement: The fallback is a product call, even if it sounds straightforward: in some cases you might not allow tagging at all unless it comes from the ML team.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it might be possible in some cases that you don't even allow people to tag unless it's coming from your ML team

statement: A student proposed updating the user's activity page with tags; the teacher (profile service activity) agreed the information is pushed asynchronously and seen by the user themself.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: should we update the user's activity page or where the user can see what happened?
flags: check: teacher called "Alok sir" just before; this label answered to "Anubhav" earlier

statement: Tags must be stored queryably: you must be able to ask in which photos a given user is tagged, so they cannot sit in an unindexable array; they go into a database that supports that query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now you cannot just have just things stored in an array, which is unindexable.

statement: You cannot pick any random database for tags: it must support the 'photos this user is tagged in' query very efficiently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just cannot pick any random database here.

statement: In startups and mid-scale companies, senior management often has not thought a seemingly simple feature through; brainstorming reveals it affects and interfaces with many other systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is what happens typically in startups and mid-scale companies where senior management has not thought it through.

statement: Feed interaction: if someone tags Arpit in a photo, should Arpit's followers get it in their feed? If yes (a product call), the feed team must gear up for the scale since every tag pushes into feeds; the feed may show such posts only to a few users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Do you want Arpit's follower to get that event right in their feed?

statement: Storing a tag's absolute pixel coordinates (e.g. 320,120 on a 720x720 image) is wrong because images are resized: on a low-end device showing it at 360x360, the tag at x=320 would land in the wrong place.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, when you do this, you cannot store 320 comma 120 in the database. Why? Because image resizing.

statement: Store the tag's relative position, e.g. 320/720 and 120/720 instead of 320,120; then, as long as the aspect ratio is maintained, the tag lands correctly at any device size. The teacher calls this a very important implementation decision.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have to tag the relative positioning of it rather than the absolute one.

statement: A tag is typically a bounding box rather than a single point, since the hover area that shows who is tagged is a region.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's typically a bounding box

statement: Two ways to store the bounding box: LTRB (relative coordinates of the left-top and right-bottom points), or X,Y of one point plus relative width and height; pick whichever the front end is more comfortable with.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: LTRB is left top and right bottom coordinates of these two points, the relative coordinates.

statement: Relative bounding boxes let the front end place the tag mapping correctly and show it on hover even when the screen shrinks, grows or resizes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And when mouse is hovered, you show it, even when your screen is like shrinking or growing and you resize and whatnot.

statement: Systems photo tagging interfaces with include search, face detection, location, notification and role-based access control (RBAC, the authorization discussed), plus analytics, profile, feed and activity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: search, face detection, location, notification, role-based access control, RBAC, role-based access control, the authorization that we spoke about.

statement: Anything the tagging service interfaces with (search, notification, analytics, profile, feed, activity) gets its events through Kafka, no matter what.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And anything that you're interfacing with, you will put it in Kafka no matter what.

statement: Think on senior management's behalf about what they have not thought about and figure out the details, because the devil lies in the details.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because devil lies in the details. Always remember.

statement: Engineers can propose product ideas: lacking product experience, they can still pitch ideas and ask the critical questions the product team would typically not have thought of.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And it is not that engineer cannot propose product ideas. Engineers can.

statement: When working with a product team or on anything user-facing, think as an end user, put yourself in their shoes and propose; that creates cross-team influence and positive impact, leading to a good career.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's how you create a cross-team influence and a positive impact in the organization, leading you to have a good career.
